title: Gambling advertising and sport

turns.speaker: Dom
turns.text: I counted the betting adverts during one match. Between the shirts, the boards and the breaks, it was over sixty separate exposures.

turns.speaker: Kiri
turns.text: For a sport a lot of eight-year-olds watch with a parent.

turns.speaker: Saoirse
turns.text: The industry line is that advertising only moves market share between firms rather than creating new gamblers.

turns.speaker: Dom
turns.text: Which would be a remarkable thing for an industry to spend that much on.

turns.speaker: Saoirse
turns.text: It's not a stupid argument in a mature market, to be fair. It's just not supported by what happens to people already in trouble.

turns.speaker: Kiri
turns.text: That's the finding that matters. Exposure has little effect on most people and a large one on the minority who are struggling.

turns.speaker: Dom
turns.text: So the average effect is small and the harm is concentrated.

turns.speaker: Kiri
turns.text: Which is how almost everything addictive works, and why averages are the wrong tool.

turns.speaker: Saoirse
turns.text: The Italian ban is the natural experiment. Total prohibition on gambling advertising, several years ago.

turns.speaker: Saoirse
turns.text: Mixed. Overall spending didn't fall much, but the clubs lost significant revenue, which is the part they talk about loudest.

turns.speaker: Kiri
turns.text: The free bet offers are what I'd target first anyway. That's not advertising, that's acquisition aimed at people who wouldn't otherwise start.

turns.speaker: Saoirse
turns.text: Narrower, more defensible, and much less satisfying as a headline.

points: A single match contained over sixty separate gambling advertising exposures, in a sport watched by children.
The industry argues advertising shifts market share rather than creating gamblers, which Saoirse concedes is not unreasonable in a mature market.
Kiri notes exposure has little effect on most people but a large effect on those already struggling, so averages are the wrong measure.
Italy's total advertising ban produced mixed results, with little change in overall spending but significant revenue losses for clubs.
Kiri would target free bet offers first, as acquisition tools aimed at people who would not otherwise start.
Saoirse agrees this is narrower and more defensible, though less appealing politically.
